    #171373. Industry News: Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1867 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the federal law known as Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding.
    • Recent findings suggest that the plaintiffs in the case are two former employees of Georgia’s state university system.
    • Machelle Joseph was the head women’s basketball coach at Georgia Tech.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the federal law known as Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding. On November 30, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument in a dispute over whether the law allows school employees to bring lawsuits alleging sex discrimination, or whether such employees must instead rely on a different federal law, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, that specifically provides a remedy for sex-based employment discrimination but also imposes constraints not found in Title IX. The employees seeking to bring the lawsuits under Title IX will face a bench that has become increasingly reluctant to permit private plaintiffs to bring lawsuits unless the federal statute at issue clearly authorizes them.

    Recent findings suggest that the plaintiffs in the case are two former employees of Georgia’s state university system. Thomas Crowther worked as an art professor at Augusta University. When he was accused of inappropriate conduct by several students, including sexual harassment, the university initially suspended him for one semester and then declined to renew his contract, prompting Crowther to file a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

    Machelle Joseph was the head women’s basketball coach at Georgia Tech. She was fired in 2019 after an investigation raised concerns about mistreatment of players. Before her termination, Joseph had repeatedly complained about her team receiving fewer resources than the men’s team. Joseph filed a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

    The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit considered Crowther’s and Joseph’s cases together. It held that Title IX does not provide a right – either explicitly or by implication – for employees to sue for sex discrimination. When the full court declined to reconsider their case, Crowther and Joseph asked the Supreme Court to weigh in, which it agreed in May to do.

    Recent findings suggest that crowther and Joseph urge the justices to reverse the 11th Circuit’s decision and allow their lawsuits to go forward. They point to the text of Title IX, which provides that “[n]o person … shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” That language, they say, creates a broad ban on sex discrimination by schools that receive federal funding; moreover, they add, Title IX “also contains ‘a list of narrow exceptions’ that does not include employment discrimination” – further evidence that Congress intended Title IX’s ban on sex discrimination to apply to both employees and students.

    The Georgia university system agrees that Title IX bars sex discrimination in employment, “and that federal agencies may deny funding to violators.” But that is not the question before the court, it stresses. Instead, it emphasizes, the problem is whether Title IX allows employees to bring private lawsuits alleging that they were the victims of sex-based discrimination. The answer, the university system notes, is no.

    To support their position, Crowther and Joseph cite several past Supreme Court rulings, including its 1982 decision in North Haven Board of Education v. Bell. In Bell, the court upheld regulations, meant to implement Title IX, that barred sex-based discrimination against employees (as well as students) at federally funded educational institutions. That decision, they say, demonstrates that Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination in employment. “The Court’s cases, read together,” they continue, “lead to the inexorable conclusion that an employee who is a victim of intentional sex-based discrimination by a federally funded education program or activity has a private right of action to seek damages under Title IX.”.

    Sources indicate that crowther and Joseph add that the Supreme Court has allowed employment discrimination lawsuits under other federal antidiscrimination statutes that apply to the recipients of federal funds – Title VI of Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color, or national origin, and the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which prohibits discrimination based on disability. Those laws, they write, contain “virtually identical” language – further evidence that Title IX allows lawsuits like theirs.

    Recent findings suggest that the university pushes back against the employees’ attempt to draw comparisons with other federal antidiscrimination laws. It writes that Supreme Court “has assumed,” but has never specifically held, that “Title VI permits private suits for the narrow category of employment discrimination that statute prohibits.” But in any event, it indicates, that assumption does not indicate anything about whether Congress created a private remedy in Title IX. The university system also emphasizes that “[t]he Rehabilitation Act has always been a far more detailed and targeted statute than Title IX” – for example, it “expressly ban[s] disability discrimination by the federal government as [an] employer.”.

    Similarly, the university system continues, the Supreme Court’s decision in North Haven Board of Education v. Bell does not resolve the question before the justices now. The court in that case, it writes, “had no reason to, and did not, consider whether Congress created a private remedy atop the express one the challenged regulations implemented.”.

    Whether the availability of another remedy forecloses private lawsuits under Title IX.

    The Supreme Court, the university system writes, has made clear that the right to bring a private lawsuit hinges on whether there is “evidence confirming that Congress sought to” provide such a right. And when Congress has created “an express remedy” in another statute, there is “a strong ‘presumption’ that Congress did not imply others” – particularly when that “express remedy” involves a “‘comprehensive’ remedial scheme.”.

    In a recent development, that is exactly what happened here, the university system argues. “Mere weeks before Congress passed Title IX,” the university contends, “it extended … [the] protection—and reticulated enforcement scheme” in Title VII to school employees, which bars employment discrimination based on (among other things) sex. Therefore, the university system says, allowing lawsuits like Crowther’s and Joseph’s to go forward under Title IX “would attribute to the same Congress an inexplicable about-face: Immediately after giving a set of employees a private employment-discrimination remedy mediated by a ‘detailed administrative and judicial process,’ it silently gave the same employees a second private right of action, to attack the same basic harm.” And it did so, the university system suggests, without requiring employees to comply with any of the “strings attached” to private lawsuits under Title VII – including, but not limited to, the requirement to first file a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission before going to court and its limits on the damages that can be recovered.

    Crowther and Joseph counter that “Title IX and Title VII are ‘vastly different.’” The prospect “that an employee might be able to bring a claim under both Title IX and Title VII does not justify” a determination that a private right of action is not available under Title IX. Rather, they write, the Supreme Court “has recognized that Congress has enacted overlapping remedies to eradicate employment discrimination, and Congress chose not to exclude employment discrimination from Title IX’s broad reach.”.

    Recent findings suggest that as additional support for the idea that Title IX does not provide a private right of action for employees, the university system notes that the law was enacted pursuant to Congress’ power under the Constitution’s Spending Clause, which gives Congress the power to impose taxes and spend money for (among other things) the country’s “general welfare.” In exchange for the federal funds, the recipients therefore agree to comply with the conditions that Congress imposes, and Congress can terminate the funding if a recipient fails to do so. However, in cases such as last term’s Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety, the Supreme Court has held that additional sanctions for violating the conditions in a law, such as the ability to bring a private lawsuit, are only available if the recipient has knowingly and voluntarily agreed to those sanctions. Here, the university system asserts, “Title IX does not unambiguously authorize private employment-discrimination suits,” and so it could not have known that it could be sued by employees, much less have agreed to that possibility.

    Crowther and Joseph reject this argument. They say that recipients of Title IX funds “‘have been on notice that they could be subjected to private suits for intentional sex discrimination under Title IX since 1979.’” As a result, they write, the Supreme Court’s “Spending Clause precedents ‘do[] not preclude private suits for intentional acts that clearly violate Title IX.’”.

    A “friend of the court” brief from West Virginia and 20 other states attempts to refute this assertion. The states tell the justices that the states “are best positioned to say what Title IX’s bargain contains, as they’re the ones who’ve accepted it.” And they “can say with firsthand authority that the deal they made did not include this,” they write. “To the contrary, all the circumstances suggested to the States that Title VII [procedures, not private lawsuits] was the rightful home for those cases.”.

    It has been revealed that the Trump administration, which filed a “friend of the court” brief supporting the university system, urges the justices not to reach the Spending Clause question at all. Instead, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer tells the justices, they “should decide this case on the ground that” the employees’ “claims fail as a matter of ‘statutory interpretation’ alone.” Therefore, he writes, it is “unnecessary to reach, and prudent to avoid, the parties’ further dispute over the constitutional notice requirement for legislation enacted under Congress’s spending power.”.

    The possible effects of the court’s decision.

    Both the Trump administration and lawyers representing public school districts warn that a ruling in the employees’ favor could have “significant adverse consequences.” The federal government suggests that allowing lawsuits like the employees’ to go forward “would crowd judicial dockets with premature lawsuits that could often be avoided through proper use of Title VII’s administrative process, which successfully resolves numerous cases. And it would undermine the government’s primary authority to enforce both Title VII … and Title IX.”.

    Industry observers note that for its part, the National School Attorneys Association emphasizes that “public school districts typically operate with limited legal and administrative staff. Expanding Title IX’s implied private right of action to cover claims against employees,” it says, “would impose disproportionate compliance and litigation burdens on public school districts and diminish the limited resources they have to educate students.”.

    But a brief from the National Education Association, supporting the employees, takes a contrary stance. It tells the justices that upholding the 11th Circuit’s decision “would remove a critical deterrent against sex-based mistreatment of educators, exacerbate an already dire workforce crisis, and ultimately compromise the quality of education available to millions of students nationwide.” Lawsuits under Title VII, it writes, are not enough because that law “does not offer the full protections to which employees of education programs are entitled.”.

    A decision in the case is expected by late June or early July.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    #171371. Court to determine if Alaska’s seizure of pilot’s plane for carrying beer violates the Eighth Amendment

    Court to determine if Alaska’s seizure of pilot’s plane for carrying beer violates the Eighth Amendment

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1775 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Tuesday in an Alaskan bush pilot’s challenge to the forfeiture of his $95,000 airplane.
    • It has been revealed that the case before the court began in April 2012, when Jouppi, who is now 83 years old, was scheduled to fly a passenger from Fairbanks to Beaver, Alaska – less than a one-hour flight.
    • In a recent development, before Jouppi took off for Beaver, state troopers arrived at the airport with a warrant to search his plane.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Tuesday in an Alaskan bush pilot’s challenge to the forfeiture of his $95,000 airplane. Prosecutors sought that forfeiture on the theory that the pilot, Ken Jouppi, must have known a passenger was bringing beer to an Alaskan village where alcohol is prohibited. That penalty, Jouppi argues, violates the Eighth Amendment’s ban on excessive fines.

    It has been revealed that the case before the court began in April 2012, when Jouppi, who is now 83 years old, was scheduled to fly a passenger from Fairbanks to Beaver, Alaska – less than a one-hour flight. Beaver, whose population was reported as 48 in the 2020 census, is a “dry” village: it bars not only the sale of alcohol, but also the importation and possession of alcohol. There are no roads to or from the village, and the closest hospital is in Fairbanks.

    In a recent development, before Jouppi took off for Beaver, state troopers arrived at the airport with a warrant to search his plane. According to the state, law enforcement officials had “receiv[ed] information that Jouppi had repeatedly transported passengers with alcohol to” dry villages. They found the equivalent of three cases of beer that his passenger was bringing to her husband, who works in Beaver, and charged both the passenger and Jouppi (as well as his manufacturer) with knowingly bringing alcohol to a “dry” village.

    The passenger pleaded guilty. Jouppi went to trial, where he was found guilty. The trial judge sentenced him to three days in prison and ordered him to pay a fine of $1,500.

    Sources indicate that under state law, prosecutors also sought to forfeit Jouppi’s plane. The Alaska Supreme Court ruled that the forfeiture did not violate the Constitution. It concluded that “the forfeiture of Jouppi’s airplane is not grossly disproportional to the gravity of the offense for which he has been convicted and, therefore … does not violate the Excessive Fines Clause of the Eighth Amendment.”.

    Recent findings suggest that jouppi then came to the Supreme Court last year. He asked the justices to decide whether, to determine if a fine violates the Excessive Fines Clause, courts should consider the gravity of the specific defendant’s conduct. The court agreed in July to take up his case.

    Jouppi and Alaska disagree on virtually every aspect of the dispute – not only the legal complications and conclusions, but also the facts. Although he denied knowing that any beer was on the plane, Jouppi characterizes the case as one hinging on just one six-pack of beer – which, state troopers testified, was visible in a grocery bag.

    According to recent reports, jouppi urges the Supreme Court to reverse the Alaska Supreme Court’s decision and send the case back to the lower court for it to take another look, stressing that “[t]he Excessive Fines Clause was built for cases like this.” He points to the Supreme Court’s 1998 decision in United States v. Bajakajian, in which the justices agreed that requiring a defendant to forfeit $357,144 for violating a federal law that required him to report that he was taking more than $10,000 in cash out of the country was unconstitutional. “As the Court has recognized,” Jouppi contends, “a forfeiture … violates the Excessive Fines Clause if it is ‘grossly disproportional to the gravity of a defendant’s offense.’” Moreover, he continues, in making that determination, courts should look at “the gravity of a defendant’s offense … not purely in the abstract, but with reference to the defendant’s own wrongdoing” – both his own culpability and “‘the gravity of the actual offense giving rise to forfeiture.’”.

    In a recent development, however, Jouppi suggests, the Alaska Supreme Court instead “evaluated [his] wrongdoing at a stratospheric level of abstraction,” by looking broadly at the harm that the plane-forfeiture law was intended to address rather than any harm that Jouppi himself might have caused by flying a six-pack of Budweiser into Beaver. When a court looks at wrongdoing “purely in the abstract,” Jouppi tells the justices, “the societal harm of even the most minor infraction will dwarf any fine imaginable.” For example, he says, in 2019, the failure to wear a seatbelt led to more than 2,000 deaths and 46,000 serious injuries, at a cost of $11 billion; the costs of speeding-related accidents amounted to $46 billion. But it would be “grossly disproportional,” Jouppi asserts, for the government to require the forfeiture of a car whenever someone failed to wear a seatbelt or went one mile per hour over the speed limit.

    In a recent development, the Alaska Supreme Court was also wrong, Jouppi continues, when it concluded that the forfeiture of Jouppi’s $95,000 plane was not grossly disproportional because that value was “only” nine-and-a-half times the maximum fine that could be imposed under state law for any class A misdemeanor, which could also include (among other things) selling alcohol to a minor, “the unauthorized practice of law, medicine, or osteopathy,” indecent exposure to a child, domestic violence in a child’s presence, “misconduct involving a corpse,” and bestiality. “That a worst-case animal abuser, or corpse abuser, or faux-osteopath could merit a $10,000 fine sheds no light on ‘the gravity of [Jouppi’s] crime’ or whether forfeiting an airplane for a six-pack is excessive,” Jouppi emphasizes.

    It has been revealed that alaska paints a very different picture, countering that “Jouppi’s crime was not flying in ‘a six-pack.’” Instead, it writes, “Jouppi loaded two cases of beer and four six-packs of 16-ounce beers on his plane destined for a village of a mere 48 people with no roads in or out and no emergency medical services.” It explains that the law allowing villages like Beaver to prohibit alcohol are a response to “the destruction caused by alcohol in its isolated, rural communities.” And because alcohol “often arrives by plane” in remote villages, state law requires a pilot who is convicted of knowingly transporting alcohol into a dry community to forfeit his plane. That penalty, the state states, both “prevents the airplane from being used again to import alcohol and deters others from doing the same.”.

    The state contends that “Jouppi fights a strawman” by “insisting that the Alaska Supreme Court considered his offense ‘purely in the abstract’”; rather, that court upheld “the forfeiture of Jouppi’s airplane … as applied to Jouppi’s actual circumstances.” In doing so, Alaska claims, it “reviewed and considered all the facts that led up to Jouppi’s conviction for knowingly transporting alcohol into a dry village. Jouppi’s actions fell squarely within the conduct targeted by the law, and he threatened to cause the same harm feared by the legislature. Whether Jouppi knew about all or just some of the nine gallons of beer he loaded onto his plane does not change the constitutional analysis.”.

    It has been revealed that moreover, the state continues, “Alaska’s forfeiture regime is not unusual or extreme.” The state points to a long history of federal laws requiring “the forfeiture of ships used to commit a host of crimes, including customs fraud, piracy, and the slave trade.” And indeed, it notes, when Alaska became a territory, “Congress imposed similar punishments” there, requiring ships to be forfeited “for the illegal killing of fur-bearing animals and the importation of alcohol. Those laws, like Alaska’s now, deterred hard-to-detect crimes and incapacitated criminals from using the vessel to repeat the offense.”.

    Finally, the state distinguishes the history of laws requiring the forfeiture of ships and planes from those involving “forfeitures of currency, such as that in Bajakajian.” Like the provision of English law on which it was based, the Excessive Fines Clause, it writes, was intended to serve as “a rebuke of ‘huge monetary penalties’ assessed by the King’s judges against his enemies.” Courts assess those penalties, the state argues, by looking at the “‘value of the fine in relation to the offense.’” But when considering “punitive forfeitures of vessels and other instrumentalities of crime,” the state stresses, the inquiry focuses on “whether the forfeiture is limited to the property ‘“tainted” by unlawful use’” – precisely the situation in Jouppi’s case.

    Like Jouppi and the state, the “friends of the court” briefs filed supporting each side take very different positions.

    A brief supporting Jouppi from the group Fair and Just Prosecution contends that “[f]ines and forfeitures in this country have evolved beyond their intended purpose of retribution and deterrence” and “now function as a revenue-generating tool that can fill budget gaps without formally raising taxes.” “Mandatory forfeiture statutes” like the one at concern in this case, the group argues, “create not only disproportionate punishments, like Jouppi’s, but also the perception that the system has self-serving goals other than public safety in mind.”.

    Another brief supporting Jouppi, from the Pacific Legal Foundation, pushes back against the idea that a court should consider the constitutionality of the forfeiture of Jouppi’s plane in light of the harm that the forfeiture law was intended to address. “The Court should analyze the confiscation of a person’s property based on individual culpability,” the group argues, “because the Constitution protects individual rights.”.

    By contrast, a “friend of the court” brief from the Alaska Legislative Council, a bipartisan committee formed to (among other things) represent the state’s legislature when it is not in session, stresses that the legislature enacted the plane-forfeiture law as “a calibrated response to a crisis unparalleled elsewhere,” “recogniz[ing] that the extraordinary isolation of rural Alaska villages, coupled with the complete dearth of public-safety infrastructure in many such communities, left residents uniquely vulnerable.” The Supreme Court, the council says, “has made clear that ‘judgments about the appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the first instance to the legislature.’”.

    Former U.S. Attorney General William Barr, along with three former Alaska attorneys general, also filed a brief supporting the state. They argue that “Jouppi’s proposed rule would” in fact “reach far beyond Beaver” to other “Alaska Native” communities, where it would “systematically understate the gravity of offenses in the communities where deterrence and prevention matter most.” Barr and the other lawyers tell the court that “[t]he question in this case is not whether six beers, standing alone, could cause every alcohol-related harm in rural Alaska. The question is whether the Constitution requires a court to pretend that Jouppi’s six beers were headed nowhere in particular, threatened nothing, and could have been conveyed by some other means. It does not.”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

We aim to empower developers by providing a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We're looking for a Head of Ecosystem to lead the teams that make Supabase the backend for the platforms and tools developers already use. That covers AI app builders and coding agents, integrations with the developer tools teams rely on, and the Supabase Marketplace. You'll build this org from the ground up and shape how Supabase extends beyond its own platform.

    You'll also drive hiring, onboarding, and career development while maintaining high engineering standards.

    Build and lead a new engineering org across platform partners, integrations, and Marketplace, hiring EMs and engineers as it grows.

    Own the technical relationship with the platforms building on Supabase, from integration health to escalations.

    Set and maintain clear roadmaps that balance partner needs with platform priorities.

    Partner with Product, Partnerships, and Sales to define and execute our ecosystem strategy.

    Ship a unified, self-serve surface for integrations and Marketplace.

    Maintain high engineering standards: roadmap hygiene, issue tracking, on-call, incident response, and responsiveness to partners.

    Proven experience leading multiple engineering teams, including managing other managers.

    Experience building and running platform, API, or integration surfaces that third parties depend on in production.

    Technical credibility with partner engineering teams, and the judgment to say no.

    Experience building teams or an org from a small base, including hiring and developing engineering managers.

    Strong organizational and execution skills: setting roadmaps, driving accountability, and keeping teams moving under uncertainty.

    Experience managing remote, globally distributed teams.

    Excellent cross-functional communication skills, especially with Product and commercial teams.

    Collaborative, low-ego, and adaptable.

    Have experience with OAuth, platform APIs, or app marketplaces.

    Have worked on a developer platform's partner or app ecosystem.

    Have worked with AI app builders or coding agents.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the firm. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are key to us.

    Once a year, the entire organization gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

    We’re looking for a Software Engineer to join our AI Tooling team and help shape how developers and agents build with Supabase. You'll build it all eval-first: every tool ships with evals and metrics, so we know, with evidence, that it makes agents better rather than worse.

    It has been revealed that you'll work closely with the Docs, CLI, Frontend and SDK teams, and with the AI Tooling Infrastructure engineers who run these services in production. Other teams contribute to AI Tooling to improve Supabase's agentic capabilities, and you'll help them do that while keeping the quality bar high.

    This role is ideal for someone who thrives in async, fast-paced environments and is excited about building developer tools that scale to millions.

    Build and improve the AI tooling we run today, including the MCP server, agent skills, agents and the Assistant.

    It has been revealed that make newly introduced Supabase products usable by agents from day one: tools, skills and evals for new product surfaces. Also build tooling for new AI technologies as they emerge: prototype swiftly, evaluate honestly, and decide with the team what is worth taking to production.

    Drive an eval-first approach: build and improve evals, instrumentation and feedback loops, measure tools against a no-tool baseline, and help define the quality KPIs and gates that stop regressions shipping.

    Understand how customers and agents actually use what we ship, and turn that into improvements to our tooling, interfaces and documentation.

    Design how documentation and product knowledge are exposed to agents, and measure whether it works.

    Build patterns and tools that help customers add AI to their own apps, such as MCP on Edge Functions, vector embeddings and agents running on Edge Functions.

    Enable teams to improve Supabase's agentic capabilities through contributions to AI Tooling: clear contribution paths, templates, documentation and review practice.

    Centralise shared AI logic so teams reuse it rather than duplicate it.

    Ship tools that are battle-tested, with strong tests, benchmarking and stress testing where it counts.

    Work with the AI Tooling Infrastructure engineers on reliability, auth and hosting.

    Work across Docs, CLI, Frontend, SDK and other teams to deliver one coherent developer experience, and stay close to the fast-moving AI ecosystem.

    Have 5+ years of experience in professional software engineering experience.

    Write strong TypeScript and know the JavaScript ecosystem well: npm, ES modules, bundlers, compatibility.

    Are deeply familiar with the AI ecosystem: current tools, agent patterns and practical trade-offs. You can tell a durable pattern from hype.

    Have built developer tools, product interfaces or platform primitives used by other engineers.

    Have designed or used evaluation frameworks to measure AI quality, reliability and task success, and understand baselines, variance and cost.

    Have strong judgement about where AI improves workflows and how to avoid fragile or gimmicky experiences.

    Write tests and validate reliability in real-world conditions.

    Know Postgres and relational database practice.

    Communicate clearly in writing, work across product, engineering and docs, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and moving promptly.

    Experience with vector databases and embeddings, ideally pgvector.

    Examples of customer-facing AI features or agents you've shipped.

    Examples of documentation or structured knowledge designed for developers or agents.

    Experience with Braintrust or a similar eval and tracing platform, or setting up CI quality gates.

    Open-source contributions or developer tooling you've maintained.

    Experience across several product surfaces or teams.

    Why Mobile Apps Treasure Downtime; Terms Of Non-Endearment

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.
    • Recent findings suggest that but wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for users’ downtime?
    • People using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.

    Recent findings suggest that but wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for users’ downtime? That’s the case made by Felix Braberg, a mobile ad and monetization consultant, in a blog post.

    People using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it. Meanwhile, both DoorDash and Uber have billion-dollar annual ad businesses, but they’re not rushing to build their own gaming or streaming offerings. So they’re natural fits for app advertisers looking to help users pass the time.

    It has been revealed that appLovin’s strength in mobile gaming is not so dissimilar. But AppLovin has a nascent consumer advertising segment now, and a few of its early advertisers have noted the power of reaching people while they’re playing games on the toilet. It doesn’t get more “downtime” than that.

    Gaming can fit neatly into the downtime vacuum that right now is awkwardly filled by ads or nothing. But successfully advertising a mobile game traditionally required a user to download the game and leave the app where they saw it advertised.

    Industry observers note that now, though, startups such as PlaysOut are integrating mobile games directly into other apps and monetizing those experiences with rewarded video. It’s a way for nongaming apps to capitalize on the downtime that benefits gaming.

    Which leads Braberg to predict that the next wave of mobile growth “will come from apps that were never game companies.”.

    Scarcely a week after launching ChatGPT’s newly introduced Business Hub, designed to let businesses see how they’re performing in ChatGPT, OpenAI has revised the Hub’s terms of service, Digiday reports.

    The revisions came soon after Digiday reached out to OpenAI, citing legal concerns brought forward by lawyers on behalf of publishers.

    Industry observers note that some of those legal restrictions have been removed in the revised terms of service. However, the revised terms also introduced more restrictions, such as requiring companies to waive their right to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data.

    It has been revealed that but, while OpenAI is still imposing some legal restrictions on companies that use its Business Hub, “they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse,” an IP and tech lawyer who requested anonymity tells Digiday. “A customer could still, even if not entirely practical, sue for monetary damages.”.

    Sources indicate that the Italian conglomerate Bending Spoons has been amassing a collection of consumer- and business-facing software vendors that kind of resembles the Island of Misfit Toys. It added another dud (or stud?) to its stable last week.

    Bending Spoons will acquire Mailchimp from Intuit for about $3.7 billion, less than a third of what Intuit paid a decade ago, Reuters reports.

    Bending Spoons also recently added the online whiteboard Miro and location-based pet-tracking service Tractive, plus once-promising internet companies Brightcove, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo and AOL. Its business model is akin to private equity, in that it acquires struggling companies and drastically reduces headcount while raising prices or removing free tiers. Interestingly, advertising is an ancillary part of its model.

    To be clear, AOL and Vimeo haven’t quit on ad revenue. But Bending Spoons is focused on subscription revenue growth and consolidated cost savings, rather than building an identity spine for advertising and data sales.

    According to recent reports, but Bending Spoons still must demonstrate that it can turn flatlined businesses (Mailchimp declined year over year, for instance) into earners. Which is a bit like trying to bend a spoon using only your mind.

    Great news on the turnaround front: Bending Spoons reported 125% revenue growth last week.

    But there’s some not-so-great news, too: Its organic growth was an anemic 3%. So growth is coming from net-new businesses, with these acquisitions contributing some $4 billion in debt.
